topic: Bike freehub: why does a bike tick when you coast? (spring pawls + internal ratchet teeth) - close variant of the ratchet winner p048
principle: The driver that carries the rear gear has spring-loaded pawls inside a ring of sawtooth teeth in the hub shell; when the wheel turns faster than the gear (coasting) the gentle slopes push the pawls down and the springs snap them back behind each steep face, which is the tick, and when the gear turns forward faster than the wheel (pedaling) the pawl tips jam on the steep faces and drive the wheel.

Why does a bike tick when you stop pedaling? 🚲

firstComment:
Answer: 2 in this model 🔧 Most bike freewheels use two or more.

Inside the rear hub, the part that carries the gears has small spring-loaded pawls, and the hub shell has a ring of sawtooth teeth around them.

Stop pedaling and the wheel keeps spinning: the teeth slide past the pawls, each gentle slope pushes them down, and the springs snap them back up behind the steep side. That snap is the tick. It's also why pedaling backward doesn't move the bike.

Pedal forward: the gear catches up with the wheel, the pawls catch the steep side of the teeth, and the wheel is driven.

(Simplified 3D model: 2 pawls, 24 teeth, slowed down, part of the gear cut away. Modern bikes usually have this ratchet in the hub (a freehub); older ones have it inside the gear cluster (a freewheel).)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Freewheel (a drum with internal teeth and two or more spring-loaded pawls; it clicks when the rider stops pedaling; pedaling forward, the pawl catches the steep slope; pedaling backward doesn't move the bike): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freewheel
Wikipedia, Freehub (the ratchet is part of the hub; the gears sit on its splined shaft): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freehub
Sheldon Brown, Freewheel or Cassette? (a cassette freehub has the ratchet mechanism in the hub body): https://www.sheldonbrown.com/free-k7.html
altText: 3D animation of a bike's rear hub on a wooden workbench, with spokes and part of the rear gear cut away. Inside the hub, two orange spring-loaded pawls sit on the dark gear carrier, surrounded by a ring of sawtooth teeth in the silver hub shell. While coasting, the wheel and its teeth turn past the still pawls, pushing them down so they snap back up with a tick. When pedaling, the gear carrier turns, the pawls catch the steep side of the teeth and the whole wheel turns with it. Then it coasts again. Text on screen: Why does it tick? Pawls. Coasting. Pedaling.
vo: Why does a bike tick when you stop pedaling?
Behind the gear, two tiny pawls sit on springs.
When you coast, the wheel's teeth push them down, and they snap back up. That's the tick.
Pedal, and they catch the steep side of the teeth and drive the wheel.
